# Incrementality and Uplift Modeling {#sec-incrementality-and-uplift}

Every model in this book so far has been trained on attributed outcomes. An install counts when the MMP credits it to an impression the DSP served, and the conversion models in @sec-conversion-prediction learn to predict exactly that. Attribution is how DSPs are evaluated and how most of them are paid, but it answers a different question from the one advertisers care about most. An advertiser wants to know how many installs would not have happened without the DSP. Some attributed installs come from users who were about to install anyway, organically or through another channel, and the DSP's impression only collected the credit.

This matters more as models get better. When I've written about pretraining deep models on non-attributed data, the step I've recommended alongside every A/B test is an incrementality holdout, because the holdout is what shows whether new signals are finding devices that your ads actually influence, rather than devices that would have installed anyway.[^c24b-intent] A model that gets very good at predicting attributed installs can get equally good at finding people who were going to install regardless.

In this chapter, we will define incrementality, show how to measure it inside an auction with ghost bids, describe the sources of randomness a DSP can use to learn it, build models that predict it per impression, and add it to the pricing equation from @sec-from-predictions-to-bids. The measurement mechanics build on the auction experiments in @sec-ab-testing-in-an-auction, and the modeling follows the same progression as the rest of this part of the book, from a simple segment-level approach to per-impression models.

[^c24b-intent]: Ben Weber, "Pretrained Deep Learning Intent Signals for Mobile DSPs," *Medium*, October 3, 2026.

## Attribution Is Not Causation

An install attributed to the DSP can happen in three ways. The DSP's ad caused it. The user would have installed organically, through a store search, a recommendation, or a chart placement. Or the user would have installed through another paid channel, and the DSP's impression won the last touch. As we saw in @sec-measurement-and-mmps, last-touch attribution credits all three to the DSP.

We split the install probability for an impression into a baseline and an uplift:

$$p_{install}(x) = p_0(x) + u(x), \qquad r(x) = \frac{u(x)}{p_{attr}(x)}$$

Here, $p_0(x)$ is the chance that the device installs without our ad, $u(x)$ is the extra chance that our impression causes, $p_{attr}(x)$ is the attributed install rate that our conversion models already predict, and $r(x)$ is the **incrementality ratio**, the share of attributed installs that are actually new.

A DSP can look excellent on attributed CPI and still have a low $r$. This happens most often when models drift toward users who are about to convert anyway, such as recent searchers, heavy players of similar games, and lapsed users of the advertiser's own app. The better a model gets at its attributed objective, the better it can get at collecting credit for installs it didn't cause.

Incrementality also has two sources, and they're worth separating. **Reach** comes from converting users that other channels don't bid on, bid too little on, or can't reach. **Persuasion** comes from changing the behavior of users that other channels also reach, through a better creative, format, frequency, or timing. Both show up as lift in a holdout test, and the segment analysis later in this chapter helps tell them apart. @tbl-c24b-terms defines the terms we'll use.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| Attributed installs | Installs the MMP credits to the DSP |
| Incremental installs | Installs that would not have happened without the DSP |
| Incrementality | Incremental installs divided by attributed installs |
| Displacement | Attributed installs that would have come from organic or other channels |
| iCPI | Spend divided by incremental installs |

: Incrementality terms. {#tbl-c24b-terms}

## Measuring Lift with Ghost Bids

A naive comparison of exposed and unexposed users is badly biased, because the bidder chose the exposed users for being likely to install. A plain holdout of users who never get ads is unbiased but diluted, since most held-out users would never have been targeted. **Ghost bids** solve both problems:[^c24b-ghost]

1. Assign each user to treatment or control with a stable hash of the device ID, for example 90% and 10%. The assignment applies to every campaign for the advertiser for the length of the test.
2. Run the full bid path for every request. Eligibility, prediction, pricing, shading, and the internal auction are identical for both groups.
3. For treatment users, submit the bid as usual. For control users, log a ghost bid with the would-be bid and its predicted win rate, and send nothing to the exchange.
4. Collect outcomes for both groups from the advertiser's complete install data, including organic and other-channel installs. Control users can never be attributed to the DSP, so attributed data alone can't be used.

![The ghost-bid design. Every request runs through the full bid path. Treatment users get real bids, and control users get a logged ghost bid that is never sent. Lift is the difference in all installs between the two groups, using the advertiser's complete install data.](../images/incr-ghost-bids.png){#fig-c24b-ghost width="100%"}

The cost of the test is only the impressions withheld from the control group, as shown in @fig-c24b-ghost. No media is spent on control users, which is the main advantage over older designs that served public service ads to a control group. Large-scale field experiments have also shown how far observational comparisons can be from randomized ones in advertising, which is a good reason to insist on randomization.[^c24b-gordon]

[^c24b-ghost]: Garrett A. Johnson, Randall A. Lewis, and Elmar I. Nubbemeyer, "Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of Measuring Online Ad Effectiveness," *Journal of Marketing Research*, 2017.
[^c24b-gordon]: Brett R. Gordon, Florian Zettelmeyer, Neha Bhargava, and Dan Chapsky, "A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook," *Marketing Science*, 2019.

### The Lift Equations

A ghost bid tells us that we would have bid, not that we would have won. So we compare all users who received at least one real or ghost bid, which is an **intent-to-treat** (ITT) comparison, and then correct for the share of treated users who actually saw an ad:

$$\text{ITT} = \bar{Y}_{T,\,bid} - \bar{Y}_{C,\,ghost}, \qquad \pi = P(\text{at least one won impression} \mid T, \text{bid})$$

$$\text{lift per exposed user} = \frac{\text{ITT}}{\pi}, \qquad \text{incremental installs} = \frac{\text{ITT}}{\pi} \times N_{exposed}$$

$$\text{iCPI} = \frac{\text{spend}}{\text{incremental installs}}, \qquad \text{incrementality} = \frac{\text{incremental installs}}{\text{attributed installs}}$$

Here, $\bar{Y}$ is the outcome rate in each group, such as installs, first purchases, or D7 revenue per user. Dividing by $\pi$ is the standard instrumental variables correction, with random assignment as the instrument and exposure as the treatment.

Let's make this concrete. Treated users who received bids install at 0.60%, and control users who received ghost bids install at 0.50%, so the ITT is 0.10 percentage points. If 40% of treated users won at least one impression, the lift per exposed user is $0.10 / 0.40 = 0.25$ points. If the DSP's attributed install rate on exposed users was 0.60%, incrementality is $0.25 / 0.60 \approx 42\%$. More than half of the attributed installs would have happened anyway, and the incremental CPI is about 2.4 times the attributed CPI.

### Displacement by Channel

When the advertiser shares the attributed channel for every install, the difference between groups splits into what the DSP added and what it displaced. @tbl-c24b-displacement shows an example per 100,000 bid-on users, assuming every treated user was exposed, for simplicity.

| Install source | Control (ghost bids) | Treatment (real bids) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Our DSP | 0 | 250 | +250 |
| Largest other network | 300 | 210 | −90 |
| Other paid channels | 100 | 80 | −20 |
| Organic | 200 | 160 | −40 |
| Total | 600 | 700 | +100 |

: Installs by source in a ghost-bid test. {#tbl-c24b-displacement}

$$\text{displacement}_c = -\Delta_c, \qquad \sum_c \text{displacement}_c = \text{attributed} - \Delta_{total}$$

The DSP is credited with 250 installs, but total installs rose by 100, so incrementality is 40%. The other 150 installs were displaced, mostly from another network, as shown in @fig-c24b-displacement. For the advertiser, those installs were paid for twice. For the DSP, the displacement shows which segments overlap with other channels, which is where to look next.

![Installs per 100,000 bid-on users by source, for the control and treatment groups. The DSP is credited with 250 installs, but total installs rise by only 100. The difference comes from installs displaced from another network, other paid channels, and organic installs.](../images/incr-displacement.png){#fig-c24b-displacement width="90%"}

### Inputs and Practical Limits

| Input | Source |
|---|---|
| User hash and test assignment | Bidder, at request time |
| Test ID, ghost flag, would-be bid, predicted win rate | Bid ledger |
| Exposure (won and billed impressions per user) | Win and billing notices |
| All installs and events for the advertiser's app, with attributed channel | Advertiser's MMP raw data, including organic |
| Spend | Spend accounting |

: Inputs to a ghost-bid test. {#tbl-c24b-inputs}

**Sample size.** Installs are rare, and lift is a small difference between two rates. For a baseline install rate of 0.5% among bid-on users and a 10% relative lift, detecting the difference with 95% confidence and 80% power takes about 312,000 users per group, with an even split and full exposure:

$$n \approx \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,p(1-p)}{\Delta^2}$$

With 40% exposure, the ITT shrinks to 40% of the lift, and the requirement grows to about 1.95 million users per group. With a 90/10 split, the total is about 10.8 million bid-on users. Report confidence intervals, not point estimates, and plan tests in weeks rather than days.

Other practical limits:

- **Complete install data.** The advertiser has to share complete install data for both groups. This is the most important request to make before a test starts.
- **Fixed assignment.** Assignment has to stay fixed for the length of the test, and across all of the advertiser's campaigns on the DSP.
- **Other channels keep running.** Other channels keep running for control users. That's correct, because incrementality is measured on top of everything else the advertiser does.
- **No device ID, no user-level test.** On iOS without a device identifier, user-level randomization isn't possible. We cover geo and switchback designs at the end of the chapter.

## Where Randomness Comes From

Uplift can only be estimated where exposure varies for reasons unrelated to the user. A DSP has three sources of that variation, and two of them come almost for free from systems the book has already built, as shown in @tbl-c24b-randomness.

| Source | What is randomized | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ghost-bid holdouts | Whether the user can be exposed at all | Withheld impressions | The cleanest source |
| Bid exploration | The chance of winning each auction | Small, already budgeted | The exploration multiplier from @sec-win-rate-and-bid-shading is an instrument |
| Near-miss auctions | Winning or losing when the bid is close to the clearing price | None | A natural experiment; needs clearing prices on both wins and losses |

: Sources of randomness for estimating uplift. {#tbl-c24b-randomness}

**Bid exploration as an instrument.** When exploration is on, the media value is multiplied by a random factor before shading, which changes the chance of winning for reasons unrelated to the user. Comparing requests with high and low multipliers gives an estimate of uplift per impression won:

$$\hat{u} = \frac{\bar{Y}_{high} - \bar{Y}_{low}}{\bar{W}_{high} - \bar{W}_{low}}$$

where $\bar{Y}$ is the outcome rate and $\bar{W}$ is the observed win rate in each multiplier bucket. This is a Wald estimator. Because exploration already runs to train the win rate model in @sec-win-rate-and-bid-shading, the DSP gets incrementality data without a separate holdout. The estimate is per impression rather than per user, and it measures the effect of one more impression at the current frequency, which is exactly what pricing needs.

**Near-miss auctions.** Requests where the bid landed just above or just below the clearing price are nearly identical, so comparing their outcomes approximates a randomized experiment. This needs clearing prices on losses as well as wins, which only some exchanges report, so it works best as a check on the other two sources.

## Incrementality Ratios by Segment

The simplest approach estimates $r$ per segment from holdouts or exploration, shrinks small segments toward the overall average, and multiplies it into the value. A segment might be an exchange, a user type (new, lapsed, payer), and a frequency bucket:

$$\tilde{r}_s = \frac{n_s\,\hat{r}_s + k\,\bar{r}}{n_s + k}$$

Here, $\hat{r}_s$ is the measured ratio in segment $s$, $n_s$ is the number of incremental installs behind it, $\bar{r}$ is the overall ratio, and $k$ sets the strength of the shrinkage. Segment ratios are coarse, but they're robust with little data, easy to explain to advertisers, and they surface the main patterns quickly. This is where I would start.

## Uplift Models

With enough randomized data, the ratio can be predicted per impression. There are three model forms, from simple to more capable.

**Two models.** Fit one model on exposed users and one on unexposed users within the randomized data, and subtract:

$$\hat{u}(x) = \hat{\mu}_1(x) - \hat{\mu}_0(x)$$

This is easy to build, but noisy, because it subtracts two estimates of rare events.

**Transformed outcome.** With a known assignment probability $e$, define a new target whose expected value is the uplift, and fit any regression model to it:[^c24b-athey]

$$Z = Y \times \frac{T - e}{e\,(1 - e)}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[Z \mid x] = u(x)$$

**Shared base with an uplift head.** A single network with two heads. The base head predicts $p_{attr}$ and trains on all data, as the conversion models already do. The ratio head predicts $r(x) \in [0, 1]$ and trains only on randomized rows, using a transformed outcome or instrumental variables loss. This is the same multi-task pattern as the conversion funnel in @sec-conversion-prediction, and it lets the uplift head borrow everything the base model has learned about users.

[^c24b-athey]: Susan Athey and Guido Imbens, "Recursive Partitioning for Heterogeneous Causal Effects," *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 2016.

### Evaluating Uplift Models

Uplift can't be observed for a single user, so the usual metrics don't apply. The standard tool is the **Qini curve**.[^c24b-qini] Rank randomized users by predicted uplift, and for the top fraction $\phi$, compute the incremental outcomes:

$$Q(\phi) = Y_T(\phi) - Y_C(\phi) \times \frac{N_T(\phi)}{N_C(\phi)}$$

where $Y$ counts outcomes and $N$ counts users in each group within the top fraction. A good uplift model rises steeply and stays above the line for random targeting. A model that ranks by attributed conversion probability often does worse than an uplift model on this curve, because it ranks users who would convert anyway near the top, as shown in @fig-c24b-qini.

![Qini curves on simulated randomized data. Targeting the top third of users ranked by predicted uplift captures about 60% of the incremental installs. Ranking by attributed conversion probability captures about the same share as random targeting, because many of its top-ranked users would install without the ad.](../images/incr-qini.png){#fig-c24b-qini width="90%"}

Also check calibration at the segment level. The average predicted $r$ in each segment should match the lift measured in that segment's holdout.

[^c24b-qini]: Nicholas J. Radcliffe, "Using Control Groups to Target on Predicted Lift: Building and Assessing Uplift Models," *Direct Marketing Analytics Journal*, 2007.

## Signals That Predict Lift

The signals that predict incrementality are not the same as those that predict conversion. Several strong conversion signals predict low incrementality, as shown in @tbl-c24b-signals.

| Signal | Direction | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency, the number of prior exposures to this advertiser | Lower lift as it rises | Each additional impression adds less. Usually the strongest single uplift feature |
| Recently lapsed users of the advertiser's app | Lower | Likely to return on their own after an update or a push notification |
| App momentum: launch week, featuring, rising chart rank, TV campaigns | Lower | A high organic baseline right now; needs a time-varying app-level baseline |
| Heavy players of very similar games, seen often in gaming supply | Lower | High intent, and heavily targeted by every other network |
| Supply where the largest networks bid most | Lower | Displacement from the same networks reaching the same users |
| Very short time from impression to install, view-through only | Lower | Often an install that was already happening, or attribution gaming |
| First few exposures to this advertiser | Higher | The ad is new information |
| Users new to the genre but engaged with apps | Higher | Interested, but unlikely to find the app on their own |
| Non-gaming supply, smaller exchanges, thinly covered regions | Higher | Fewer competing exposures |
| Rising intent in recent bid-stream activity | Higher | Reaching users before other channels flag them; see @sec-sequences-and-transformers |
| Playable and rewarded formats | Higher | More likely to change behavior rather than collect credit |

: Signals that predict lift. {#tbl-c24b-signals}

The inputs come from the DSP's own bid stream (which apps and exchanges a device appears in, which also proxies exposure from other networks), the exposure log (frequency, recency, creative, format), the advertiser's data (lapsed status, the organic install curve), and app-level time series (chart rank, featuring, seasonality).

## Pricing on Incremental Value

The incrementality ratio enters the pricing equation from @sec-from-predictions-to-bids as one more term in the advertiser value, before shading. There are two ways to use it, and the advertiser should choose, because they're billed on attributed outcomes:

$$\text{tilt:} \quad A = 1000\,\kappa\,p_{attr}\,V \times \big(1 - \alpha + \alpha\,r(x)\big)$$

$$\text{incremental goal:} \quad A = 1000\,\kappa\,p_{attr}\,r(x) \times T_{iCPI}$$

Here, $A$ is the advertiser value per thousand impressions, $\kappa$ is the calibration multiplier, and $V$ is the value of an install under the campaign's goal, such as its target CPI. With the **tilt**, the campaign keeps its attributed goal, and $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ sets how strongly low-lift segments are discounted. Attributed CPI rises slightly, and incremental installs per dollar rise. With an **incremental goal**, the advertiser sets a target cost per incremental install, $T_{iCPI}$, and bids are priced on uplift directly. This mode suits advertisers who run their own lift tests and trust them over last-touch numbers.

The pacing system in @sec-pacing-and-budget-control works the same way with either form, because it only sees the value. Two notes are worth keeping in mind. The calibration multiplier $\kappa$ corrects bias in attributed predictions and doesn't measure incrementality, so the two terms are separate. And with an incremental goal, the goal controller measures surplus on incremental outcomes, which arrive only through holdouts and exploration, so its slow loop runs on test readouts rather than daily cohorts. @tbl-c24b-pricing lists the new pricing inputs.

| Input | Symbol | Source | Default to start |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incrementality ratio | $r(x)$ | Segment table or uplift model | 1 |
| Tilt strength | $\alpha$ | Campaign, advertiser opt-in | 0 |
| Incremental CPI target | $T_{iCPI}$ | Campaign, advertiser opt-in | Not set |

: Pricing inputs for incrementality. {#tbl-c24b-pricing}

## Incrementality on iOS

Without a device identifier, users can't be randomized, and outcomes can't be joined per user. Two designs still work:

- **Geo holdouts.** Randomize regions, such as US designated market areas, into treatment and control, and compare total installs and revenue per region from the advertiser's data. Use matched pairs or synthetic controls to reduce noise, and run long enough to cover weekly cycles.
- **Switchback tests.** Turn the DSP on and off in alternating time blocks within a region, and compare outcomes across blocks. This works when effects fade quickly, and is weaker for goals with long windows.

Both designs give lift for a campaign or a region rather than per user, so they support segment-level ratios but not per-impression uplift models. @sec-ios-and-contextual-signals covers the broader constraints of working with limited signals on iOS.

## How the Industry Approaches Incrementality Today

Most large platforms optimize on attributed outcomes and leave incrementality to measurement. Meta is the main public exception. It introduced an incremental attribution setting that optimizes delivery for conversions its models predict were caused by an ad, as an alternative to its standard attribution, and has expanded it since its initial launch in 2025.[^c24b-meta] Other platforms have partnered with independent measurement firms, so that advertisers can run lift tests on their campaigns. Explicit uplift-based bidding is still the frontier, for three reasons: uplift labels are rare and noisy, holdouts cost revenue, and advertisers' dashboards and MMPs report attributed outcomes.

For a smaller DSP, this is an opportunity. A DSP that measures lift with ghost bids, reports displacement honestly, and offers an incremental goal has something to sell that scale alone doesn't provide.

[^c24b-meta]: "Meta Updates Information on Incremental Attribution Conversion Tracking," *Social Media Today*, <https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/meta-updates-information-incremental-attribution-conversion-tracking/>

## Conclusion

Attributed outcomes tell a DSP which installs it got credit for. Incrementality tells it which installs it caused. In this chapter, we split the install probability into a baseline and an uplift, measured lift inside the auction with ghost bids, found two more sources of randomness in systems the DSP already runs, and built models that predict the incrementality ratio, from segment tables up to a shared network with an uplift head. The ratio enters the pricing equation as one more term before shading, either as a tilt on an attributed goal, or as an incremental goal the advertiser chooses.

The practical order is the same as elsewhere in the book. Start by measuring lift with holdouts for a few advertisers who share complete install data. Use the results to build segment-level ratios and to report displacement honestly. Turn on the exploration-based estimates as the randomized data grows, and move to per-impression uplift models once there is enough of it. In the next chapter, we return to the bid landscape and the win rate model, which the exploration data in this chapter also trains.
